overview: Turkmenistan is a living sovereign state, not a synonym for every Turkmen person or every society that once occupied this part of Central Asia. Independence was proclaimed on 27 October 1991 within the former Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic’s borders, but the atlas begins its layer in 1994. That three-year lag is a map convention, not a second founding. The 1994, 2000, and 2010 files reuse one detailed 219-position polygon. The modern layer replaces it in 2020 with a simplified 54-position polygon. Both are approximate display geometry, not legal boundary surveys. Coverage records four consecutive intervals, while the civilization index leaves the ending open. Within that frame, the card uses dated sources for government, work, water, households, schools, health, and sanitation. Those sources describe laws, surveys, programmes, places, and practitioners, so the card does not turn one example into every citizen’s experience. Its modern identity begins with independence, not with every earlier settlement inside its present borders. The atlas’s 2100 renderer horizon predicts nothing. Turkmenistan and its people continue beyond the latest evidence cited here.

periods.title: The atlas arrives after independence
periods.summary: The first Turkmenistan feature appears in 1994, three years after the 1991 declaration of independence. Earlier sampled places are painted as the Soviet Union. The band closes with the United Nations General Assembly recognizing and supporting Turkmenistan’s declared permanent neutrality on 12 December 1995.

periods.title: Neutrality accompanies concentrated rule
periods.summary: Presidential power remained highly concentrated after permanent neutrality became a central diplomatic status. A 1994 referendum had extended Saparmurat Niyazov’s term; in December 1999 the legislature named him president for life. The dated background note also describes one legal party and weak institutional checks during this period.

periods.title: Personalized government narrows public life
periods.summary: Niyazov’s life presidency anchored an intensely personalized political system. Contemporary background reporting described one legal party and weak institutional checks. This editorial band ends at the alleged 2002 assassination attempt, after which the documented crackdown marks a useful evidence boundary, not a change in the country’s mapped border.

periods.title: Repression and service closures precede succession
periods.summary: The Library of Congress profile describes arrests and tighter controls after the 2002 alleged attack, along with Niyazov-era closures of hospitals outside Ashgabat and rural libraries in 2005. Niyazov died in December 2006. Those events changed government and services, while the state and its people continued.

periods.title: A new president takes office
periods.summary: ODIHR’s 2017 report dates Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow’s first presidential election to 2007 and his re-election to 2012. This period records a change in officeholder without claiming an institutional restoration. UNESCO listed the Parthian Fortresses of Nisa in 2007, recognizing ancient remains inside the modern state.

periods.title: A longer term inside a controlled system
periods.summary: Constitutional changes adopted in 2016 lengthened the presidential term from five to seven years and removed the upper age limit for candidates. The 2017 election occurred in what ODIHR described as a controlled environment without genuine opposition or political pluralism.

periods.title: Living heritage and an early election
periods.summary: UNESCO listed Kushtdepdi in 2017, carpet making in 2019, and dutar craft and performance in 2021. These listings document living practitioners, not universal habits. On 12 February 2022, President Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow called for power to pass to young leaders; a 12 March election was scheduled, with his son Serdar among nine candidates.

periods.title: The state continues beyond the map horizon
periods.summary: ODIHR’s report dated 9 October 2023 identifies Serdar Berdimuhamedow as president and finds that the March 2023 parliamentary election lacked genuine competitiveness and pluralism. UNESCO listed Akhal-Teke horse-breeding and decoration traditions in 2023. The atlas extends rendering to 2100, but no source here predicts events or an ending.

sections.title: Read the modern state and its map carefully

items.text: The index starts Turkmenistan in approximately 1994, although independence was recognized on 27 October 1991. The Library of Congress dates that independence to the referendum day. The offset belongs to the imported atlas timeline, so 1994 should never be presented as the republic’s founding year.

The 1994, 2000, and 2010 files contain the same Polygon: one ring, 219 stored positions, 218 unique vertices, and one geometry hash. A reused outline is evidence about the atlas’s cartography. It does not prove that every boundary marker stayed physically unchanged for twenty-six years.

The modern GeoJSON replaces the earlier outline with one simplified ring of 54 positions and 53 unique vertices. Its bounding box shifts slightly. Ashgabat, Mary, Turkmenabat, Dashoguz, Balkanabat, and Turkmenbashi remain inside both shapes, showing continuity through a renderer change rather than a political rupture.

In the three historical TopoJSON snapshots, decoded shared arcs meet Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Iran, and Afghanistan, one arc each. Representative probes find no ownership overlap for the target feature. These tests check atlas topology; they are not a substitute for treaties, surveying, or border administration.

Coverage records four intervals through a 2020-to-2100 renderer band, matching three historical files plus the modern layer. The index remains open-ended. The number 2100 is a display horizon, not a forecast, expiration date, or invitation to invent a future fall of Turkmenistan.

sections.title: Follow institutions without mistaking ceremony for consent

items.text: United Nations resolution 50/80 A, adopted without a vote on 12 December 1995, recognized and supported Turkmenistan’s declared permanent neutrality and asked member states to respect it. The resolution establishes an international diplomatic act; it does not measure domestic opinion or election quality.

A United States Department of State background note records that the legislature made Saparmurat Niyazov president for life in December 1999. It also describes earlier term extension by referendum. These dated institutional facts explain concentrated rule without treating one leader’s personal cult as ordinary Turkmen family life.

After Niyazov died in December 2006, constitutional manoeuvring allowed Deputy Prime Minister Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow to stand in the February 2007 special election, which he won. The Library of Congress profile was completed that month, so its account captures the transition without pretending to know its later outcome.

The March 2022 election was called early after Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow announced a leadership transition. ODIHR conducted a remote needs assessment rather than observing election day. Its report records extensive presidential powers, rights concerns, and limited pluralism; those findings should remain tied to that mission and date.

A January 2023 law re-established the Halk Maslahaty with broad stated powers and membership. ODIHR’s election report found that all registered parties supported the president and offered no genuine alternatives, while parliament’s role was further reduced. The official law and independent assessment answer different questions.

sections.title: Work with gas, farms, roads, and hard choices

items.text: Natural gas, oil, and oil products supplied 84.9 percent of total exports in 2024, according to the World Bank. Gas wealth shapes national revenue and infrastructure, but a percentage about exports says little about how income, shortages, or opportunity feel inside any particular household.

State-owned enterprises accounted for 59.2 percent of total turnover in 2023. The World Bank also calls for better public resource management, fiscal transparency, and accountability. Those cautions matter because official growth figures and national totals are difficult to interpret when underlying public data are limited.

Agriculture employed 42.5 percent of the labour force in the World Bank’s current overview, while facing low productivity, water scarcity, deteriorating soil, rising temperatures, and salinity. Farming is therefore both a major source of work and a daily contest with an arid environment.

For a landlocked country, roads, railways, ports, and trade logistics connect production to neighbours and the Caspian. The World Bank treats better connectivity as part of economic diversification. A map may show four land neighbours neatly, but moving goods requires working systems far beyond coloured borders.

In Dashoguz, a UNDP story follows communities facing drought, salinity, and waterlogged fields. Residents added household fruit and vegetable gardens, kept cattle for milk and yoghurt, and worked through local leaders. It is a project account, not proof that every farmer had the same experience.

sections.title: Meet daily life through documented living practices

items.text: In Turkmenistan’s translated national-inventory registration card for Nowruz, families and communities prepare cereal foods, especially semeni, a thick wheat porridge, for the spring equinox celebration. Children play named games while music and dance accompany three days of events. Semeni is festive food, not evidence for everyone’s breakfast.

UNESCO’s carpet entry describes hand-woven wool on horizontal or vertical looms, with coloured geometric patterns associated with five main Turkmen tribes. Carpets may cover floors or walls and appear at births, weddings, prayers, and mourning. Even a carpet can have a busier calendar than many people.

Turkmen-style needlework begins by twisting three layers of fine silk thread, then forming loops with a thin needle. Regional motifs decorate wedding and funeral clothes as well as scarves, coats, trousers, shawls, and accessories. UNESCO documents a flexible craft, not a mandatory national uniform.

A dutar is a long-necked, two-stringed lute whose pear-shaped body and soundboard are made from mulberry wood and whose neck uses dried apricot wood. Makers hollow, polish, dry, glue, fret, string, and tune it. Performers bring it to ceremonies, festivals, and social gatherings.

Kushtdepdi combines sung wishes, vocal improvisation, hand movements, gestures, and steps shaped by the tune. Communities perform it at ceremonies and national celebrations. Master singers and dancers teach through oral and practical work, while music schools and cultural centres also support learning.

sections.title: See families, celebrations, and care across generations

items.text: Carpet knowledge is transmitted within families, while the annual Carpet Day brings weaving communities together. UNESCO also records special carpets for a child’s birth, weddings, prayer, and mourning. These occasions show textiles participating in family life without proving that every household owns or makes each kind.

Akhal-Teke traditions include naming, racing, riding, beauty contests, and decorated wedding horses. UNESCO says women primarily create and transmit the jewellery and lace used for decoration. Young breeders learn contact, grooming, feeding, riding, and training through formal and informal instruction.

UNICEF’s early-learning centres brought young children and parents together weekly and added home visits. Facilitators used familiar activities, including cooking and weaving, to demonstrate counting, patterns, fine-motor practice, and conversation. The point was not tiny homework sheets; it was learning through things families already did.

The 2015-2016 household survey estimated that 0.2 percent of women aged 15 to 49 had married before 15 and 5.9 percent of women aged 20 to 49 before 18. These are survey estimates with sampling limits, not permission to label individual families.

A ten-week positive-parenting pilot worked through twenty-four preschools, twenty-four trained educators, and about 250 parents. Sessions emphasized communication, play, daily routines, and preparing children for school. The reported scale is modest and specific, useful precisely because it is not inflated into a nationwide claim.

sections.title: Learn in Turkmen and make room for every child

items.text: Written sample: “Adam hukuklary güni gutly bolsun!” The paired United Nations page translates it as “Happy Human Rights Day!” It is modern Latin-script Turkmen, so romanization is identical and no transliteration is needed. This 10 December 2025 web sentence is not an ancient inscription.

Article 21 of the Constitution states that Turkmen is the state language and guarantees every citizen the right to use a mother tongue. The education law makes Turkmen the principal instructional language while also promising support for mother-tongue and foreign-language learning. Law text shows rules, not implementation by itself.

UNICEF’s education fact sheets use household survey data to show large regional and wealth differences in foundational reading and numeracy, alongside unequal access to computers and the internet. National enrolment alone cannot tell whether children can practise skills or reach digital materials at home.

UNICEF’s situation analysis reports that many children with disabilities or functional difficulties were outside educational institutions, using the most recent evidence then available. The finding exposes an inclusion gap; it should not be turned into a claim that those children were incapable of learning.

A joint assessment identified sixteen students at School 74; multidisciplinary teams at the four pilot facilities started developing tailored individual education plans. The release does not report completed plans or family participation. Sixteen is a pilot count, not a national total for the country.

sections.title: Use clinics, surveys, and family-centred care

items.text: The health ministry and UNICEF launched the nationwide rollout of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses programme in March 2025. The approach links provider skills, health-system support, and family and community practices. A national launch does not prove that every child immediately received identical care.

WHO reported that maternal mortality had fallen by about 80 percent and under-five mortality by nearly 45 percent since 2000. Those national trends mark substantial progress, while still requiring continued prevention and care. A falling rate is good news, not a reason to stop asking who is missed.

Mengli, a child with cerebral palsy, and his mother travelled about six hours to an early-intervention centre. UNICEF describes physical and speech therapy delivered by a multidisciplinary team with family participation. One family’s journey makes both the value of care and the distance barrier visible.

The national micronutrient survey sampled 2,672 households, including urban and rural locations, and interviewed women while collecting data about women and children. It examined diet, feeding, anaemia, iodine, iron, folate, and vitamins A and D. That is nutrition detective work with laboratory tools.

UNICEF says vaccine cooperation began in 1994 and that Turkmenistan finances essential vaccine procurement, including HPV vaccination for girls and boys. Cold-chain equipment helps doses survive the trip from storage to clinics. The chain is literal: vaccines dislike getting warm much more than children dislike waiting rooms.

sections.title: Look closely at water, waste, toilets, and clean hands

items.text: The 2015-2016 MICS estimated that 82.8 percent of household members used improved drinking-water sources. Its detailed table separated water piped into a dwelling, plot, or yard from other improved and unimproved sources. A national percentage therefore hides large differences in how water reached homes.

The same survey estimated 98.6 percent used improved sanitation facilities that were not shared; its tables distinguish flush systems, ventilated improved pits, slab pits, and other arrangements. “Improved” is a survey category, not a promise that every toilet was comfortable, nearby, or continuously supplied with water.

For children aged zero to two, 60.5 percent of last stools were disposed of safely in the survey, with sharp regional variation. This question matters because a household can have an improved toilet while infant feces follow another route. Tiny humans create surprisingly serious sanitation statistics.

School handwashing sessions used glitter to show how pretend germs travel among hands, books, apples, cups, and other surfaces. Videos and online sessions reached schools nationwide. Glitter is usually invited to celebrations; here it became a cheerful villain that refused to stay politely in one place.

UNDP estimates that agriculture consumes 88 percent of the country’s water and that about half is lost between withdrawal and delivery because of old irrigation infrastructure and inefficient management. Those estimates concern the water system, not household blame. Modern irrigation pilots test ways to waste less.

sections.title: Protect ancient places and living achievements

items.text: Ancient Merv preserves a succession of oasis cities spanning roughly four millennia. It became an Abbasid capital in the ninth century and a Great Seljuk capital in the eleventh and twelfth. UNESCO listed the park in 1999; the ruins are heritage within Turkmenistan, not the modern republic’s birth certificate.

Old and New Nisa preserve one of the Parthian Empire’s earliest important centres. Excavation has revealed richly decorated domestic, state, and religious architecture at a crossroads of trade and strategy. UNESCO’s 2007 listing honours Parthian evidence without relabelling ancient residents as citizens of a twentieth-century state.

Kunya-Urgench contains monuments mainly from the eleventh through sixteenth centuries, including a minaret about sixty metres high. UNESCO traces its architectural influence across Iran, Afghanistan, and later Mughal India. The site’s reach reminds us that ideas travel more freely than tidy modern border colours suggest.

The 866-kilometre Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor links component sites in Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. UNESCO’s 2023 inscription follows routes used from the second century BCE to the sixteenth century CE. Shared nomination is an achievement in protecting a connected history that no current country owns alone.

UNESCO listed Akhal-Teke horse-breeding and decoration practices in 2023. The entry celebrates knowledge held by breeders, riders, craftspeople, women who make decorations, and young learners. An inscription recognizes living practice; it does not turn every resident into a rider or every horse into a national monument.

sections.title: Continue past the last dated map and statistic

items.text: At 2020 the renderer swaps a detailed historical polygon for simplified modern geometry. Most tested cities remain inside, and the id stays Turkmenistan through the renderer horizon. A point near Serhetabat changes sampled owner because of simplification. That is a map edge warning, not a diplomatic incident.

Decreasing precipitation, rising water shortages, desertification, and salinity threaten farming and rural livelihoods. UNDP reports that more than 60 percent of rural people depend on agriculture and that women are especially vulnerable. Current adaptation work includes solar pumps, efficient irrigation, and locally planned responses.

UNDP’s Dashoguz project began with local knowledge and community leaders, then supported drainage cleaning, training, gardens, crops, and livestock livelihoods. The account shows adaptation as practical work rather than a slogan. It also stays honest about place: project villages cannot represent every farm in Turkmenistan.

Children in UNICEF’s MyDream campaign imagined becoming a veterinarian, footballer, pilot, author, and even a pizzeria owner. Their answers are individual voices from a campaign, not a scientific poll. They are still valuable: a country’s future is also made of wonderfully specific plans for grown-up life.

ODIHR’s 2023 assessment records tightly controlled media, limited internet access, restricted fundamental freedoms, and no genuine political alternatives among registered parties. These are serious dated findings about institutions. They do not erase the agency, creativity, relationships, or ordinary work of people living under those conditions.

ending.text: There is no fall to narrate. Turkmenistan remains an independent state, and the atlas record has no historical end date. Its final geometry band runs from 2020 to 2100 because the renderer needs a future ceiling; that number does not predict borders, leaders, climate, or daily life. A UNICEF release published on 29 January 2026 instead documents a continuing five-year Country Programme for 2026 to 2030, launched at an event held the previous day. It names child survival, health and nutrition, inclusive education, child protection, social policy, participation, and climate resilience as programme priorities. The same release reports outcomes from the preceding 2021 to 2025 programme: training for 5,000 health professionals, immunization coverage above 95 percent across fourteen vaccines, early-childhood services for more than 80,000 children, complex social support for more than 7,000 families, and Green School pilots in twenty schools. These are UNICEF programme claims about reach and plans, not proof that every need has been met or every resident has the same experience. The card therefore ends with dated institutional evidence and living continuity. The map’s future ceiling is only software. Turkmenistan’s next history belongs to the people who will live it.
